verses.text: In the third year of the reign of king Belshazzar a vision appeared to me, even to me, Daniel, after that which appeared to me at the first.
I saw in the vision; now it was so, that when I saw, I was in the citadel of Susa, which is in the province of Elam; and I saw in the vision, and I was by the river Ulai.
Then I lifted up my eyes, and saw, and behold, there stood before the river a ram which had two horns: and the two horns were high; but one was higher than the other, and the higher came up last.

I saw the ram pushing westward, and northward, and southward; and no animals could stand before him, neither was there any who could deliver out of his hand; but he did according to his will, and magnified himself.
As I was considering, behold, a male goat came from the west over the surface of the whole earth, and didn’t touch the ground: and the goat had a notable horn between his eyes.
He came to the ram that had the two horns, which I saw standing before the river, and ran on him in the fury of his power.

I saw him come close to the ram, and he was moved with anger against him, and struck the ram, and broke his two horns; and there was no power in the ram to stand before him; but he cast him down to the ground, and trampled on him; and there was no one who could deliver the ram out of his hand.
The male goat magnified himself exceedingly: and when he was strong, the great horn was broken; and instead of it there came up four notable horns toward the four winds of the sky.
Out of one of them came out a little horn, which grew exceeding great, toward the south, and toward the east, and toward the glorious land.
It grew great, even to the army of the sky; and some of the army and of the stars it cast down to the ground, and trampled on them.
Yes, it magnified itself, even to the prince of the army; and it took away from him the continual burnt offering, and the place of his sanctuary was cast down.
The army was given over to it together with the continual burnt offering through disobedience; and it cast down truth to the ground, and it did its pleasure and prospered.

Then I heard a holy one speaking; and another holy one said to that certain one who spoke, How long shall be the vision about the continual burnt offering, and the disobedience that makes desolate, to give both the sanctuary and the army to be trodden under foot?
He said to me, To two thousand and three hundred evenings and mornings; then shall the sanctuary be cleansed.
When I, even I Daniel, had seen the vision, I sought to understand it; and behold, there stood before me as the appearance of a man.
I heard a man’s voice between the banks of the Ulai, which called, and said, Gabriel, make this man to understand the vision.
So he came near where I stood; and when he came, I was frightened, and fell on my face: but he said to me, Understand, son of man; for the vision belongs to the time of the end.
Now as he was speaking with me, I fell into a deep sleep with my face toward the ground; but he touched me, and set me upright.
He said, Behold, I will make you know what shall be in the latter time of the indignation; for it belongs to the appointed time of the end.
The ram which you saw, that had the two horns, they are the kings of Media and Persia.
The rough male goat is the king of Greece: and the great horn that is between his eyes is the first king.
As for that which was broken, in the place where four stood up, four kingdoms shall stand up out of the nation, but not with his power.
In the latter time of their kingdom, when the transgressors have come to the full, a king of fierce face, and understanding dark sentences, shall stand up.
His power shall be mighty, but not by his own power; and he shall destroy wonderfully, and shall prosper in what he does; and he shall destroy the mighty ones and the holy people.

Through his policy he shall cause craft to prosper in his hand; and he shall magnify himself in his heart, and he shall destroy many in their security. He shall also stand up against the prince of princes; but he shall be broken without hand.
The vision of the evenings and mornings which has been told is true: but seal up the vision; for it belongs to many days to come.
I, Daniel, fainted, and was sick certain days; then I rose up, and did the king’s business: and I wondered at the vision, but no one understood it.

footnotes.content: Daniel's visions keep coming—this is the third such moment in King Belshazzar's reign. Notice how he says 'even to me, Daniel,' as if still amazed that the Lord speaks to him this way. A man receives what he cannot predict; he learns to trust the voice that calls.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Susa was a grand royal city, capital of Elam; standing by the Ulai river, Daniel is transported in vision to this place far from Jerusalem. The Lord shows him not the temple where he wishes to dwell, but the seat of earthly power—to teach him what matters and what will fall.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Two horns on the ram: one high, the other higher still. Even in a vision, Daniel sees how power rivals itself, how one kingdom overtakes another. He's watching the shape of history itself—and learning that earthly crowns rise and fade like the grass.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The ram pushes everywhere—west, north, south—and nothing stands against him. 'He did according to his will,' the text says plainly. A kingdom unopposed by any rival grows proud, and pride is always the moment before the fall. The Lord lets us see it coming.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A goat 'didn't touch the ground'—extraordinary speed, as if carried on air itself. The notable horn between his eyes speaks of a singular ambition, a force with one burning purpose. Daniel watches the very shape of conquest, and it is swift and strange beyond measure.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: 'Ran on him in the fury of his power'—the goat moves with a violence that's almost alive. Watch how quickly the mighty ram, so confident in verse 4, now faces his match. The Lord shows us that no strength stands forever; there is always one who comes after.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The ram's two horns are broken, he's cast down and trampled. The swiftness of his defeat matches the swiftness of his rise. Even the mightiest kingdom cannot stand before the one the Lord allows to come. This is not revenge; it's the pattern of history itself.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The goat 'magnified himself exceedingly'—the old pride now claims the victor's place. But see: at the height of his strength, his great horn is broken, and four horns rise in its place. The Lord teaches Daniel that no single kingdom holds forever; all power is temporary, all pride is prelude to scatter.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: From one of the four horns, a little horn grows 'exceeding great,' reaching toward the south, the east, the glorious land. A small beginning, yet it grows and reaches—and grows toward the place God loves. Daniel is watching the shape of desolation approach.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: 'Cast down some of the army and of the stars'—this horn reaches even toward heaven itself, claiming dominion over things spiritual. It tramples the very signs and servants the Lord sends. Yet notice: it does not touch the throne. It rises high, but there is always a limit.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The horn 'magnified itself, even to the prince of the army'—it dares to affront the Lord himself. It takes away the continual offering, casts down His sanctuary. This is arrogance beyond measure, and Daniel sees it written in vision. Yet the Lord shows it first to His prophet—He does not leave His people in ignorance.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: 'Cast down truth to the ground'—when power severed from God's will takes root, it corrupts the very soil where truth grows. The Lord allows this not out of weakness, but to show us what a world looks like when it forgets Him. He lets us see the bitter fruit of such forgetting.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The holy ones speak to one another—the heav'nly court is watching too. They ask 'How long?' This is the question that echoes through exile and sorrow: how long will the Lord permit this? And notice they ask it of each other, as if in wonder. Even the holy ones are turned toward the answer.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: 'Two thousand and three hundred evenings and mornings'—a precise number, a sealed span of time. The sanctuary will be cleansed. Not destroyed forever, but restored. Here the Lord plants a seed of hope in Daniel's heart: there is an appointed end to desolation, a morning after the night.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Daniel seeks to understand—a natural impulse when the vision presses on the mind. 'Behold, there stood before me as the appearance of a man.' The Lord does not leave His prophet confused. He sends one who will explain, who will make clear what the vision means. Our Father does not speak and then silence us.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Gabriel is called by name—the mighty one who 'makes the man understand the vision.' Gabriel means 'God is mighty,' and his task is to translate heaven's speech into the human heart. When we are overwhelmed, the Lord sends an interpreter, one who knows both the divine intention and our frail understanding.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Daniel falls on his face in fear—this is not a gentle vision, but one that shakes the soul. Yet Gabriel tells him 'Understand, son of man; for the vision belongs to the time of the end.' He does not diminish the fear, but places it in the frame of God's purpose. The vision shows an ending—and that is mercy.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Daniel falls into deep sleep, his face to the ground—the burden of what he has seen is more than his frame can bear. Gabriel touches him, sets him upright. How gentle: the messenger does not leave him prostrate, but lifts him to receive what comes next. Even in heavy things, the Lord steadies us.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: 'The latter time of the indignation'—the Lord's wrath on human pride, always time-appointed, never eternal. It is an indignation bounded by His mercy, given form by His justice. Gabriel will now unveil what Daniel's heart needs to carry: knowledge of the shape and season of what comes.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The ram is Media and Persia, its two horns the joint kingdoms that ruled the world Daniel knew. This is not fanciful allegory—these are the kingdoms of history, given divine interpretation. God knows the names and shapes of human rule; He reads them as a parent reads the games children play.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Greece is the goat, and the great horn between his eyes is its first king—likely Alexander, who swept across the known world with a speed that seemed almost impossible. Yet here, in a vision given centuries before, the Lord names him. Your future is known to Him, even when it rushes toward you unforeseeable.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: 'Four kingdoms shall stand up out of the nation, but not with his power.' After Alexander's death, his empire fragmented into four—never as mighty as under his hand. Even kingdoms that conquer the world cannot hold unity after their founder. Only the Lord's kingdom endures.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: 'A king of fierce face, and understanding dark sentences.' This is a ruler of cunning and violence, skilled in deception. He comes 'when the transgressors have come to the full'—pride and sin bear fruit, and from that fruit such a man arises. The Lord lets us see how evil germinates in the soil we ourselves prepare.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: 'Not by his own power'—mark this well. The tyrant thinks himself strong, but the Lord tells us the truth: his power is granted, not inherent. He destroys, he prospers in what he does, but only because the Lord permits it for a season. Even the mighty one has a master.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: 'Shall stand up against the prince of princes; but he shall be broken without hand.' Here is the resting place for Daniel's heart and ours: no weapon, no earthly force breaks this tyrant. It is the Lord Himself—'without hand'—who crushes him. Our King cannot be defeated by any power made of flesh.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: 'The vision of the evenings and mornings is true, but seal up the vision; for it belongs to many days to come.' The Lord confirms what Daniel has seen—not imagination, but truth. Yet He seals it: not for Daniel alone, but for all who will read it in ages not yet born. We inherit the reassurance meant for the exiles.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Daniel fainted, fell sick—the weight of knowing what he knows, of holding such a vision in a mortal frame. Yet he rose and did the king's business, lived his daily life, carried the secret. Readers today hear an echo: sometimes we too must carry the weight of what the Lord shows us, live faithfully, and wait in silence for His time.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
